title: Plato: The Republic, Books VI–X
short: The philosopher-ruler, the divided line, the cave, how cities decline, and the myth of Er.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
In the second half of the Republic, Socrates tells the most famous story in all of philosophy: the cave.

Imagine people who have lived their whole lives chained in a cave, facing the back wall. Behind them a fire burns, and people walk past carrying cut-out shapes of animals and things. All the prisoners ever see are the shadows of those shapes on the wall. They give the shadows names and think they are the real world.

One day a prisoner is set free. He turns around and sees the fire, which hurts his eyes. Then he is pulled up a steep path, out into the sunlight. At first he is dazzled. Little by little he sees reflections in water, then trees and animals, then the stars, and at last the sun itself. Now he knows the truth!

blocks.name: gb-cave
blocks.cap: Step through the story, from the chains to the sunlight and back.

blocks.html: He goes back to tell the others. But his eyes are not used to the dark anymore, and the prisoners laugh at him and don't believe him. Plato says that learning is like this: turning around and climbing toward the light, even when it is hard.

🧩 Try this

Shadow theater. In a dark room, shine a flashlight at a wall and make shadows with your hands or with paper cut-outs. Can someone guess what each shadow is? Which shapes are hard to guess? Talk about what the prisoners in the cave could never know just from shadows.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Book V ended with Socrates' boldest claim: cities will have no rest from trouble until philosophers rule. Books VI and VII explain what a philosopher is and how one is educated. Socrates first tells a parable of a ship whose owner is strong but deaf and short-sighted, and whose sailors fight over the wheel and call the one man who studies the stars and winds a useless stargazer. That, he says, is how cities treat the real experts in ruling.

blocks.text: The sun, the line and the cave

blocks.html: Asked what the highest thing to know is, Socrates says it is the Good, but he can describe it only through images. The sun gives light so that eyes can see things and makes them grow; in the same way the Good gives truth to what the mind knows and makes it what it is. Then he draws a divided line: things seen (images, then real objects) and things known (mathematics, then the Forms).

blocks.cap: Change the ratio. The two middle parts, things and mathematics, always come out the same length.

blocks.html: Then, in Book VII, the cave:

blocks.name: gb-cave
blocks.cap: The five stages of the story. Compare the cave with the divided line: shadows, things, and finally the sun.

blocks.html: Reading the cave. The shadows are like images and opinions taken on trust; the objects carried past are like the things we see; the world outside is like the realm of the Forms; and the sun is like the Good. Socrates says the prisoners are “like ourselves.”
Socrates draws a lesson about teaching. Education is not putting knowledge into an empty mind:

The future rulers study arithmetic, plane geometry, solid geometry, astronomy and harmony, all to turn the mind from the changing to the unchanging, from about twenty to thirty, and then five years of dialectic, the art of question and answer. Then they must go back into the “cave,” serving in public life for fifteen years, and only at fifty take their turn at ruling. Socrates says the best rulers are those who do not want to rule.

blocks.text: Books VIII–IX: how cities and souls decline

blocks.html: Socrates describes how even the best city would decay, step by step, each kind of city matched by a kind of person: rule by the wise gives way to rule by lovers of honor (timocracy), then to rule by the rich (oligarchy), then to democracy, which he says loves freedom so much it loses all order, and finally to tyranny. The tyrant, ruled by his own worst desires, is the least happy of all. These are Plato's judgments; later thinkers, including Aristotle, classified governments differently.

blocks.text: Book X: poets and the myth of Er

blocks.html: Socrates returns to the poets. A painter's picture of a bed copies a carpenter's bed, which copies the Form of a bed, so the painting is “third from the truth.” He would allow only hymns to the gods and praise of good people in the city, though he invites poetry's defenders to answer him. The book ends with the story of Er, a soldier who came back to life and told how souls choose their next lives. The wise choice, he says, is the one that makes the soul more just. The soul of Odysseus, tired of ambition, looks for the quiet life of an ordinary person.
Reading the cave as only about one person's escape. Socrates insists the freed prisoner must go back down and help the others, even though it is hard and he would rather stay in the light.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The cave has been retold more than any other story in philosophy, in sermons, novels and films. It asks whether the world we see is the real one, and what it costs to find out. Some read it as a story of religious awakening, some of science, and some of education. Augustine, later on this ladder, read Plato's sun and light as pointing to God as the light of the mind; Descartes asked how we can know our senses are not deceiving us.

Aristotle, Plato's student, doubted that the Forms are separate from things, and studied the changing world directly, as the science rungs of this ladder show. Others object that the cave makes ordinary people prisoners and gives too much power to those who claim to see the light. Plato's defenders answer that the freed prisoner goes back to serve, not to rule for himself.

items: Have you ever found out that something you believed was only a “shadow”? How did it feel?
Is it kind to drag someone out of the cave who doesn't want to go?
Why might the best rulers be the ones who don't want to rule?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. If you had lived all your life in the cave, would you believe the person who came back? Why or why not?
  2. What are some “shadows” today: things people see that aren't the whole truth?
  3. Why did the freed prisoner go back into the cave? Would you?
  4. Socrates says a teacher doesn't put knowledge into you but turns you toward it. Has a teacher ever done that for you?
  5. The freed prisoner's eyes hurt at first. Is learning something new sometimes uncomfortable?
  6. In the story of Er, souls choose their next life. What would you look for in a life?
